content: Clinical studies have been conducted to evaluate the outcomes in patients using analogue insulin compared to human insulin. Long-acting insulin analogues have demonstrated statistically significant reductions in HbA1c levels and a decreased risk of nocturnal and severe hypoglycemia compared to human insulin. Short-acting insulin analogues, as reviewed in a recent Cochrane analysis, showed only minor benefits in glucose control for individuals with type 1 diabetes. Patient preferences and treatment satisfaction are increasingly recognized as critical goals in diabetes management. Validated tools have been developed to assess these aspects, but a systematic review of patient preferences has not yet been performed. This review aims to identify differences in adult patient preferences between conventional human insulin and insulin analogues in individuals with type 1 diabetes. A PubMed search was conducted using terms related to type 1 diabetes, insulin, satisfaction, stated preference, and decision analysis. Studies focusing exclusively on children and adolescents, those without English text, or those lacking full-text availability were excluded. Additionally, studies investigating inhaled insulin or newer technologies like artificial pancreas systems were excluded due to their limited widespread use. Comparisons of preferences between various insulin injection devices (e.g., pens vs. syringes) were also excluded, as both analogue and human insulin are available in vials and cartridges. The initial search yielded 1,017 citations, and 16 studies were included in the review. Eight studies compared rapid-acting analogues with short-acting human insulin, four compared long-acting analogues with intermediate-acting human insulin, two compared both rapidand long-acting analogues with shortand intermediate-acting human insulin, and two compared biphasic human and analogue insulin. Among the studies comparing rapid-acting analogues and short-acting human insulin, six reported significantly higher satisfaction scores with analogue insulin, while two found no difference. None of the studies reported higher satisfaction with human insulin. All four studies comparing long-acting analogues with intermediate-acting human insulin found significantly higher satisfaction with analogue insulin. Of the studies comparing both rapidand long-acting analogues with shortand intermediate-acting human insulin, one found a preference for analogue insulin, while the other found no difference. Neither of the two studies comparing biphasic human and analogue insulin found a difference in patient satisfaction. One of these studies was a double-blind trial involving patients with type 2 diabetes, included here due to the limited evidence from blinded studies. Factors contributing to improved treatment satisfaction included greater flexibility in treatment or diet, convenience, improved quality of life or well-being, reduced perceived hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, improved blood glucose stability, and increased energy levels or reduced fatigue. Patients in several studies expressed satisfaction with continuing analogue insulin or recommending it to others. Other reasons for improved satisfaction included increased physical strength, perceived protection from long-term complications, better overall well-being, easier daily activities, more balanced glucose control, reduced worry, improved emotional status, and reduced impact of diabetes on life (e.g., family relationships, role functioning, and social networks). Overall, 11 of the 16 included studies reported that patients preferred analogue insulin over human insulin, with a stronger preference for long-acting analogues. However, these results should be interpreted cautiously due to the high risk of bias in most studies, as only two were double-blinded. Patients participating in studies comparing novel interventions with standard treatments may have a predisposition to favor the new treatment, potentially influencing their behavior and appraisal of the treatment. It is important to note that neither of the double-blinded studies found a significant difference in patient satisfaction between human and analogue insulin. Double-blinded studies are challenging to conduct due to differences in pre-meal injection timing recommendations for analogue and human insulin. However, multiple studies have shown that patients tend to inject at similar times regardless of the type of insulin used. Blinded studies also have limitations, as they do not account for treatment flexibility and convenience, which are important factors in treatment satisfaction. Only one study considered patient preference and treatment satisfaction as a primary outcome, with most studies focusing on clinical endpoints and satisfaction as a secondary outcome. This makes it difficult to distinguish between satisfaction arising from treatment characteristics versus satisfaction due to improvements in clinical outcomes such as HbA1c. Two studies found that treatment satisfaction was associated with a decline in HbA1c, and one study found that patients were more likely to prefer analogue insulin if their baseline HbA1c was above the median in the study population. In conclusion, most studies indicate that patients prefer analogue insulin over human insulin. However, almost all studies focused on clinical endpoints, with treatment satisfaction as a secondary outcome. Greater emphasis on the patient experience is needed, as this affects both the perceived burden of diabetes and the likelihood of adherence to recommended treatments and achieving optimal glycemic control. Given the high risk of bias in most included studies, higher-quality evidence is required before definitive conclusions can be drawn. Future studies should consider designs that incorporate patient preferences to reduce bias, minimize dropouts, and maximize adherence to study protocols.
